<reason>B won the central clash over mandatory completion within five years. A established credible efficiency benefits from replacing subsidies, but B distinguished unequal subsidy shares from the actual purchasing-power losses facing excluded households. B supplied measurable readiness conditions, accepted temporary leakage, and explained why its alternative could capture reform benefits without overriding failed delivery. A’s deadline-as-discipline argument never adequately answered that comparison. Its premature accusations that B had ignored questions, including a nonexistent reference, also misread the chronology and weakened its rebuttal.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s strongest response targeted A’s “We proceed” answer: gradual price increases and years of registry-building do not compensate the particular family that receives nothing. This directly defeated A’s attempt to treat phased implementation as an answer to failed delivery.</best_rebuttal>
